questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I've spent time abroad in England beforehand and loved the experience. So it was very natural for me to go to Scotland as an extension of that experience. I've always loved the idea of Scotland and wante to experience the culture and people myself.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
It was ok. Their systems can be quite tricky to work out - especially getting courses was a very tedious process.
I'd encourage others to not put too much faith in getting their initially approved courses. I thought I'd be able to have courses outside of my faculty (Sociology) - but that was not allowed. Neither were Master-level courses which was a shame.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Assistance in picking courses - but only due to how convoluted the process was.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Housing situation is abysmal. Not even students who were guaranteed (+1 Erasmus students) housing could get it. We had to rent AirBnB's for the time - as did many others. There are rooms available through 3rd-party sites, but these are VERY hard to come by so be on the lookout way ahead of your travels.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If possible, live in the West End - this is were the university is. The Southside (south of River Clyde) is pretty dodgy and I would not recommend living there alone. Public Transport is a joke: subway closes 11:30pm all days of the week so living close to campus or city center is a must if you plan on going out (and not paying for Ubers).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Don't count on getting housing from the university - it's a shitshow. Try finding other student accomodations like flatshares - otherwise there are off-site student accomodation... but these are VERY expensive relative to what you get.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Had to fill out an arrival form - which was easy enough.
Then I had to show up to an office where I was officially registrered and got my student ID - pretty easy overall

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not much - they're very busy upon student arrival so communications are very hard to come by

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Getting classes is terrible. As an international student you are second in line to choose courses (Glasgow Uni's own students get to pick first) so many courses are already filled when they're available to Erasmus Students.
The enrollment process is also way too tedious - you have to send a lot of emails and accept the fact that you will probably have to select at least 2 new courses. 
The course catalogue provided by the university is also not up to date - at least it does not properly show which courses are available on what semesters. So just have in mind that you will have to settle on some courses you might not have thought to take.
You are also not allowed to do Master-level courses. While there are certainl interesting courses on their Bachelor's it is a shame not to have that possibility - especially because it narrows the amount of courses available to international students drastically.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Don't put too much faith in getting your pre-approved courses.
Have patience - the enrollment is VERY slow and VERY tedious. You might not have any courses at all until October depending on your (un)luck.
And don't choose Master courses - you won't get them.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Not Masters

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: A lot of it was very good - in smaller classes with about 30 people. Lecturers were very passionate and immensely knowledgeable which is great.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Understanding Empire
Contemporary Debates in Media Sociology
Quantitative Methods in Social Sciences

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Understanding Empire - It's an amazing course on Imperialism and it's consequences taking both a very historical and sociological view of mechanisms and causes of Imperialism and how consequences manifested from this. THe course lecturer, Andy Smith, is an absolute delight to have and is so passionate about teaching - I'd recommend any course he teaches.

If you are interested in media sociology take Contemporary Debates in Media Sociology - it's a great course as well with a very good lecturer.

DO NOT TAKE THE QUANTITATIVE METHODS COURSE - IT IS AWFUL

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Generally - high housing costs and public transportation, as well as Ubers.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food is cheap compared to Denmark - even their vegan options (like meat replacements) can be found pretty cheap if you look in the discount shops (Iceland, Farmfoods).

Pints are also cheaper!!!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There are loads of clubs and associations to join on the uni - I'd recommend going to the sports clubs' taster sessions were you can try out the different sports.
Don't feel bad if you don't have the time to properly join though - there's loads to do anyways

Join the walking society if you're interested in smaller hikes

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Find a good pub with a good pub quiz! They're all over town and is a great way to spend an evening with your friends.
Join the gym - it is decently priced for students - but it is absolutely huge - and comes with a swimming pool, sauna, steam room and free spinning classes!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
GO TO THE HIGHLANDS.
There are student organized trips - like going to Isle og Skye
See if you can climb some the higher mountains (called Munroes).
Visit Edinburgh

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy if you enjoy drinking pints

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Everyone is friendly and striking up conversation is very easy. If you want to socialise more - join a sports club or an association
there's also a Nordic Society if you feel homesick

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: They drive in the wrong side of the road,so biking is not recommended

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Friendliness

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go to the highlands at least once - it is truly beautiful
Go to the Old Toll Bar on the Southside (by Kinning Park station) - Seriously it's THE BEST BAR in Glasgow by far, and has something going on everyday (live music, dj's etc.) And their wednesday pub quiz is amazing. I am not kidding go there. at least once.
There's always something to do in Glasgow - whether it be going to pubs, joining a sports club or a society - find something that interests you and stick to it. You will probably not get around to everything on your bucket list.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Whisky tastings! Go on a tour of the Clydeside Distillery!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Making new incredible friends

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Housing - make sure you're looking out for rooms early

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
